prize_parts.citation: For a body of fiction in Chinese in which dream logic dismantles ordinary psychology, space and causality, and renews the possibilities of narrative invention.

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change: Can Xue (B001), single-writer citation. It is, however, narrower and more conditional than it was in round 1. The case rests on three criteria. Distinctiveness of voice: the dream logic in works such as Frontier and Love in the New Millennium is a kept formal principle, not a decorative surrealism, and it displaces conventional psychology and causal plot. Formal and linguistic achievement: invention lies in how each narrative world is built, which does not depend on a national, testimonial or topical frame. Sustained quality and depth: the project has been pursued for decades with real imaginative and intellectual seriousness. The citation should rest on the fiction, with her critical writing as supporting evidence only, as Palm said in round 1. Nothing in round 1 gave a specific reading showing variation within the method, so that question remains open for me. I do not read it as decisive against her, because the work is compressed, so repetition costs less than in very long cycles, and because the method looks like the work itself and not a surface style. This is a close judgment, not a verified finding. I take no account of nationality, language, gender, symbolism or the number of colleagues who agree. My own earlier stated interest in women's authorships is not a ground for this choice, and I do not rely on it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and still unanswered: range against intensity. If the dream-logic method does not deepen or vary across the later novels, or if the long works do not hold up as well as the best short fiction, an oeuvre that is hermetic through its whole length would weaken the case under the criteria of sustained quality and significance. I cannot judge the Chinese original. Only part of a very large corpus is available to me in translation, and the translators' share in how the prose reads is large. I have not independently verified any text. The colleagues who support Cărtărescu make a serious competing argument for scale, register and a project that keeps widening, and the committee has not yet tested it against Can Xue on the page. If evidence emerged that her later work only restates the early method, I would move to Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg keeps Cărtărescu first because his project seems to vary more in scale and register while keeping its identity. He also suggests a citation that centres the novels and treats the poetry as a foundation, since the poetry is thinly covered in translation.
responses.response: His suggestion about citation scope is sound. A citation resting on Blinding and Solenoid would be more defensible than one that claims a unity of prose and poetry that few of us can check. That makes the Cărtărescu case more precise, and it is one reason he remains my first alternative. I am still not persuaded that wider scale is a stronger sign of sustained quality than formal discipline held over decades. Scale is exactly what has to be tested against the repetition concern that he himself names for the long late volumes. I accept his point that the choice is close and could go either way. What would move me is a reading showing that the later Cărtărescu widens the project and does not circle it, or a reading showing that Can Xue's later novels do the opposite.

responses.point: Mattson answers the repetition worry by reading Solenoid as an enlargement of scale and register. She asks the committee to read across the later volumes and not only the best-known novels, and she says she would move Can Xue to first if Cărtărescu's later work thins.
responses.response: I accept that test and apply it in both directions. Her reading of Solenoid as extension, not restatement, is the best answer in the file to the excess concern, and I cannot refute it from public knowledge. Where I still differ is on what the density of the longer form shows. The recurrence of motifs could be architecture or thinning, and the shift from the Blinding trilogy to later work is something I know mainly through reception. I would take her offer of symmetry. If readers can show that Can Xue's long novels vary within the method, I stay with her. If they show recurrence without development there, and Mattson's reading of Cărtărescu holds, my order should reverse. No one has yet supplied that evidence, so my first place stays provisional.

responses.point: Carlberg places Can Xue first and rests the case on the rigour of the dream logic. She also says the long works may divide opinion, and that if the long works do not sustain the invention of the best short fiction the case would weaken considerably.
responses.response: I agree with her on rigour and on the translation limits, and I again note that our agreement is not an independent check. We are both reading the same translated sample and public description. Her conditional is the clearest statement of what would change my position, and I would add one practical point for the committee: the stories and the novels should be assessed separately, because a judgment formed on stories alone cannot support a claim about sustained quality in the novels. I also share her caution about Robinson only in part. I still see the sentence-level control and the Gilead sequence as real achievements, but a compact fiction corpus in one deeply explored world gives a narrower significance claim than the one I want in a whole-oeuvre recommendation.

responses.point: Olsson, as chair, keeps Zurita first and argues that the claim rests on the sequences' syntax, imagery and architecture, with the sky-writing and desert works as context only. He names Can Xue as a close second he would accept on literary merit.
responses.response: I take his condition seriously, and I find it more workable than I did in round 1: a citation confined to the books of poetry would keep the extra-textual works out of the claim. My difficulty is not the seriousness of the project but verification. A non-Spanish reader can judge the architecture of the sequences far more easily than the language, and the language is where he places the merit. I have not seen a close account of the verbal achievement of Purgatory or Anteparadise, and I cannot supply one. His willingness to accept Can Xue on literary grounds matters to me as a statement about her case, but I do not use it as evidence of merit. For now Zurita stays outside my alternatives, and I would reconsider only if Spanish-language readers can show that the later volumes sustain the early intensity.

uncertainties: Whether Can Xue's later novels deepen or vary the dream-logic method or restate it; no specific reading was supplied in round 1, so this remains unresolved.
How much of her very large Chinese-language output is available in translation, and how far the translators shape the voice; I cannot judge the original and have not verified any text.
Whether the long novels sustain the invention of the best short fiction, which I think the committee should test separately.
Whether Cărtărescu's late long volumes extend or restate the earlier project, and whether his poetry, thinly translated, can be counted as an equal part of a citation.

How non-textual work (Zurita), essays and scholarship (Robinson, Carson), and a career-long reshaping of a poetic language (Adonis, known to me mainly through critical reputation) should be weighed under common criteria.
Comparing poets, hybrid writers and novelists under one set of criteria remains imprecise, and my judgments rest on public information and translations, not independent verification.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own literary practice (family drama, love and obsession, WWII-era refugee fiction) is context only and shows no connection to any shortlisted writer. My professional ties are to fellow Academy and committee members, not to any candidate. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
